cards.text: Jerusalem has fallen, and God's people have been carried off to Babylon (2 Kings 25:8-11). This psalm looks back on that time. It opens by the rivers of Babylon, where they sat and remembered Zion.

cards.question: By the rivers of Babylon, God's people remember Zion. What do they do there?

cards.text: There on the willows, they hang up their harps. I think I know a little about going quiet, friend: in the junk drawer I went a good while without one single joke, and now look at me, I can't STOP.

cards.question: The captives hang their harps on the willows in Babylon. What was going on there?

answers.text: Their captors demanded songs of joy
Their harps had all broken strings
Their leaders told them to stay silent

cards.question: The captors don't want just any song. They want the captives to sing a song about Babylon.

cards.text: Picture your boss catching you on your worst day: "Come on, SMILE! Tell everybody something FUN!" Then the psalm asks a question of its own.

cards.question: The psalm asks how they can sing a song of the LORD in a ___ land.

cards.text: Now the "we" turns into "I." The singer speaks straight to Jerusalem, like the city could hear every word.

cards.question: The singer speaks to Jerusalem and starts with an "if." What is that "if" about?
If the singer ever forgets Jerusalem, the singer asks for a right hand that stops working and a tongue stuck to the roof of the mouth.
The captors demanded songs of joy. But the singer calls Jerusalem the singer's greatest ___.

cards.text: Then the singer turns to the LORD and brings up the sons of Edom, the people who came from Esau (Genesis 36:9). It goes back to the day Jerusalem fell.

cards.question: On the day Jerusalem fell, what were the sons of Edom saying about the city?

answers.text: Tear it down to its foundations

cards.question: The singer asks the LORD to forget what the sons of Edom said the day Jerusalem fell.

cards.text: There's that word again: remember. Now the singer turns to Babylon itself: "O Daughter of Babylon, doomed to destruction"

cards.question: The singer says the one who repays Babylon is ___.
The singer calls the one who repays Babylon blessed. Repays Babylon in what way?

answers.text: As Babylon has done to them
With silver and gold for their losses

cards.text: Then comes the last line, and it's the hardest one in the psalm: "Blessed is he who seizes your infants and dashes them against the rocks." That's where the psalm ends, friend, and it doesn't tidy anything up.

findings.problem: The opening card gives the historical setting but never identifies who is speaking the psalm or to whom. The speaker is not introduced until the singer is mentioned on card 8.

rule.text: The opening card can be up to 3 sentences. It says who is speaking, to whom, and what is going on. If the passage starts in the middle of a thought, it gives the context.

findings.problem: The question types follow a repeated formula: multiple choice, true or false, then fill in the blank on cards 4, 5 and 7; again on cards 9, 10 and 11; and again on cards 13, 14 and 16.

rule.text: No formula. Which question type comes next, the order the types come in and where a blank falls are chosen naturally for each card. They never follow a pattern. No stop repeats another stop's pattern, and no type dominates a stop by a wide margin.

findings.problem: The standalone question does not identify who "they" are. It should name God's people or the captives rather than relying on context from an earlier card.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.
